title: Francis, again
tomorrow: who stays up all night talking with an innkeeper, and why?

segments.voice: The week, looking back down the mountain. Catherine called the pope home: always renewing. Bakhita found a different master: saints of our time. A name on every page of the year: every day, someone. A shepherd with pipes: four pillars. A competitive streak, aimed: grace perfects. And yesterday's first word, the one Benedict and the Shema share: listen.
screen: `ALWAYS RENEWING.` → `SAINTS OF OUR TIME.` → `EVERY DAY, SOMEONE.` → `FOUR PILLARS.` → `GRACE PERFECTS.` → `LISTEN.`

segments.voice: Clearing out a closet can feel like losing something, or like finally breathing. In Assisi, a cloth merchant's son has been giving his father's money to the poor and to a crumbling church. The father hauls him before the bishop to get it back. And the son, Francis, does more than return the money. Thomas of Celano, who wrote his life, says he took off his clothes, right there, and handed them back too. The bishop covered him with his own cloak.
screen: `A CLOSET: LOSS, OR BREATHING?` → `BEFORE THE BISHOP.` → `HE HANDS BACK HIS CLOTHES.`

segments.voice: Why? Because Francis wanted nothing standing between him and God, not even a father's name stitched into his clothes. And his poverty wasn't grim. Francis sang. He wrote the Canticle of the Creatures, praising God through brother sun, sister moon, even sister death. Jesus says, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven." Francis took that literally and lightly at once. Where did the gladness come from? In his Testament, Francis says that while he was still in his sins, the sight of lepers was bitter to him. Then the Lord led him among them, and what had seemed bitter turned into sweetness of soul and body. Giving up the distance came first. The joy came after. The one to tell a friend: Francis wrote the Canticle in his everyday Italian, not in Latin, and it's a song of thanks, not of loss. Poor and glad: empty hands, and room to receive.
screen: `NOTHING BETWEEN HIM AND GOD.` · `BROTHER SUN, SISTER MOON.` · `BLESSED ARE THE POOR IN SPIRIT.` · then, large: `POOR AND GLAD.`

segments.voice: Reach for one thing within arm's length that you could live without, and set it to one side, ready to give away. Then hold your empty hand open for the rest of the sit. If you pray, you can thank God for one thing you already have, the way Francis thanked him for the sun.
Francis. The merchant's son from Assisi who gave everything back, and sang.
Pocket this one: poor and glad, empty hands with room in them for what God gives next. Another week, done.

howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of Francis of Assisi on October 4, often with blessings of animals; Franciscan friars and sisters take a vow of poverty and pray his Canticle of the Creatures.

chat.says: giving my old cleats to the freshman i yelled at. Mia says that's sad, like i'm quitting. is it?
options: Not sad. Francis gave things away and sang. It's making room, not quitting.
Kind of. Giving up things you love always means losing a part of yourself.
Only if you're giving them to look good. Otherwise just keep your cleats.
chat.meaning: Francis's poverty was glad, not grim: he gave everything back and praised God through the sun and moon. Empty hands have room in them.
